The Tzemach Tzedek told them: “We polish buttons with sand and water, and we polish our neshamos with sand and water, as well. The sand is the words of Tehillim, and the water is the tears we shed while saying them. When saying Tehillim with tears, we polish our neshamos.”

Rosh Hashana is an appropriate time for all of us to polish our neshamos with lots of Tehillim.

The Tzemach Tzedek once traveled to a group of Jewish soldiers called “Cantonistim” who had been drafted into the Russian Army. They were so excited for the Rebbe’s visit that they arranged a whole parade for him!

One of the soldiers came over to the Rebbe, crying. He said, “Rebbe, we polished our buttons for you. Now, please polish our neshamos!”

It’s always important to greet other people with nice words, but on Rosh Hashana, it is actually a minhag. It’s even written about in the machzor! We have a special greeting—to a boy or man, say: “וְתֵחָתֵם לְׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּתִּכָתֵב”, and to a girl or woman, say: “וְתֵחָתֵמִי לְׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּתִּכָתֵבִי”. They both mean, “May you be written and sealed for a good and sweet year!”

When we say this to each other, even the malachim are excited to hear it. The Tzemach Tzedek said that when the two malachim hear us bentching our fellow Yid with a good and sweet year, they go up to Shamayim and demand that Hashem bentch us with a good and sweet year, as well!

Rosh Hashana is the special Yom Tov when we crown Hashem as King. We chassidim have our own minhagim

for this holy time: We write a Pan to the Rebbe before

Yom Tov, say a specific bracha when bentching licht, and are sure to wish each other “L’shana tova” at night.

One of the most important ways that a chayol prepares for the new year is by writing a נֶפֶׁש ּפִדְיֹון, called a “נ”ַפּ”, to the Rebbe. A Pan is not just a letter. It is a way to express the deep neshama-connection between a chossid and a Rebbe. In a Pan, we ask the Rebbe to daven to Hashem for us.

We try our best to bring our Pan to the Ohel in person, but if we can’t, we make sure to send it in time for Rosh Hashana. Before writing a Pan, men put on a gartel, and everyone thinks carefully about what they want to tell the Rebbe.

Rosh Hashana is not just any Yom Tov. It is the day when we crown Hashem as King, and remind Him of our special bris with Him.

As Chabad chassidim, we declare how special Rosh Hashana is as soon as it begins—right when we bentch licht!

Many Yidden say “לְהַדְלִיק נֵר ׁשֶל יֹום טֹוב—to light the candle of Yom Tov,” but the Rebbe explains that our minhag is to say “לְהַדְלִיק נֵר ׁשֶל יֹום הַזִּכָרֹון—to light the candle of the Day of Remembering,” specifically mentioning one of Rosh Hashana’s special names. By doing this, we help the ko’ach of the day come down and be revealed even more!

Have you ever seen a courtroom? It is a serious place where everyone sits quietly, waiting for the judge to decide the ruling. Rosh Hashana is like the court case for the whole world, and so it is a serious time. It’s so serious that some Chabad chassidim are careful not to talk at all for the entire Rosh Hashana! The minhag of our Rebbeim was mainly not to talk throughout the first night of Rosh Hashana.

But we don’t just sit quietly doing nothing. Instead of talking, we say Tehillim. We try to fill every spare moment of Rosh Hashana with these holy words. The Frierdiker Rebbe encouraged all chassidim to sleep less and spend more time learning Torah and saying Tehillim. We make sure to add at least a little extra time saying Tehillim on this holy and serious day.

What’s your favorite part of the Rosh Hashana meal? For many people, it’s the apple dipped in honey!

Our minhag is to dip the apple in honey right after kiddush. We say the bracha of “Ha’eitz”, and then, before taking a bite, we add, “יְהִי רָצֹון מִלְפָנֶיָך ׁשֶּתְחַדֵש עָלֵינּו ׁשָנָה טֹובָה ּומְתּוקָה—May it be Your will [Hashem] that the new year be good and sweet for us.”

Many people have the minhag to say the Yehi Ratzon after first eating some of the apple. The Alter Rebbe even says to do that in his Shulchan Aruch! But in Hayom Yom, the Rebbe notes that we say it before eating, and explains in a letter that this causes the Yehi Ratzon to become part of the bracha itself. You see, a bracha has more power to make things actually happen in this world than a Yehi Ratzon does. So, by including the Yehi Ratzon in the bracha of “Ha’eitz”, we give it the same super-power as a bracha, making sure that our new year will be good and sweet for sure!

Whenever children come to shul and answer “אָמֵן” and “יְהֵא ׁשְמֵי'ה רַּבָה”, powerful malachim are created. But the Rebbe says that on Rosh Hashana, it’s even more powerful and important to do so! Precious Yiddishe children saying these words with the minyan can tip the scales of Hashem’s judgment, and bring a good year to the entire world.

Let’s be sure to come to shul and answer “amein” loudly and clearly!
